clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) was used to explore associations between GMV asymmetry deviations and clinical/behavioral scores separately for ASD without DD/ID and ASD with DD/ID groups. Statistical significance was tested through 10,000 random permutations. Canonical loadings (threshold ±0.2) were calculated to determine contributions of brain regions and clinical measures. For ASD without DD/ID, one significant mode (r=0.977, p_perm=0.033) linked asymmetry deviations with clinical scores including ADOS, visual responsiveness, verbal communication, interaction, and independent living scores. For ASD with DD/ID, one significant mode (r=0.988, p_perm=0.003) linked deviations with both clinical scores (CARS, SRS, ABC, SM subscales) and IQ scores (verbal IQ, performance IQ). Group comparisons used one-sample t-tests (FDR q<0.05) and two-sample t-tests between patient groups. Kurtosis analysis identified regions with extreme individual variability. Spatial correlation analysis with spatial permutation tests (n=10,000) assessed between-group similarities. Unsupervised clustering (k-means, t-SNE) was performed to explore group separability. Gene expression associations were analyzed using partial least squares (PLS) regression and inter-regional similarity analysis with spatial permutation tests and bootstrapping (n=10,000) to identify genes contributing to asymmetry patterns.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Young children with ASD (1-7 years) showed rightward GMV asymmetry in the inferior parietal lobe and precentral gyrus, and higher individual variability in the temporal pole; ASD with DD/ID had more extensive abnormalities linked to both ASD symptoms and verbal IQ, while ASD without DD/ID showed higher heterogeneity linked only to ASD symptoms; DD/ID children showed no significant asymmetry deviations.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling on 1030 children under 8 years (775 ASD, 36 DD/ID, 219 TD), the study found ASD-common patterns of more rightward GMV laterality in the inferior parietal lobe and precentral gyrus, and higher individual variability in the temporal pole. ASD with DD/ID children (n=563) exhibited more extensive abnormalities with negative deviations (more rightward) in precentral (t=-5.58, p<0.001), inferior parietal (t=-4.5, p<0.001), fusiform (t=-3.9, p=0.0012), and entorhinal (t=-3.4, p=0.0062), plus positive deviations (more leftward) in bank of superior temporal sulcus (t=2.94), isthmus cingulate (t=2.91), paracentral (t=2.82), and rostral anterior cingulate (t=2.8). ASD without DD/ID children (n=212) showed negative deviations in precentral (t=-4.84, p<0.001) and inferior parietal (t=-4.36, p<0.001), positive deviation in rostral middle frontal cortex (t=3.59, p<0.01), and extreme kurtosis (>5) in 10 regions including temporal pole (k=41.451), parahippocampal (k=50.502), entorhinal (k=64.391), and fusiform (k=31.153). DD/ID only children (n=36) showed no significant deviations. Canonical correlation analysis revealed distinct brain-behavior associations: ASD without DD/ID showed one mode (r=0.977, p=0.033) linking asymmetry with ASD symptoms only; ASD with DD/ID showed one mode (r=0.988, p=0.003) linking asymmetry with both ASD symptoms and verbal IQ. Spatial correlation showed significant similarity between ASD with DD/ID vs. ASD without DD/ID (r=0.557, p=0.0007) and ASD with DD/ID vs. DD/ID (r=0.741, p<0.0001). Gene expression analysis identified shared GO terms across all patient groups (regulation of transmembrane transport, neuron projection development, axon, supramolecular fiber organization) and unique terms for each group, with inter-regional similarity analysis showing significant associations (ASD with DD/ID: r=0.16, p=0.0001; ASD without DD/ID: r=0.216, p=0; DD/ID: r=0.241, p=0).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: VBM methodology limitations; normative model only included age and sex as covariates, not environmental factors like socioeconomic status; gene expression data from healthy adults used for children's brain-transcriptome associations; unbalanced sex ratio limiting sex-specific analyses; most subjects scanned under sedation with different proportions between groups; lack of multimodal functional imaging data
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: GMV in current study is obtained by automated morphology method called voxel-based morphometry (VBM). The performances of segmentation and registration in preprocessing are key factors on accuracy of VBM. ... the normative model extracting GMV asymmetry deviations only considered the effects of age and sex. Environmental factors, such as socioeconomic status, may also affect the brain morphology development ... limited by the availability of gene expression data, we linked GMV asymmetry deviations in 1to 7-year-old children to transcriptional profiles from healthy adults ... the sex ratio of this work is unbalanced, which limits the exploration about sex effects on developmental disorders. ... Most of our subjects were scanned during sedation-induced sleep. The proportions of sedation in ASD and DD/ID children are higher than that in TD group. ... functional brain variants also play an important role in the multimodal cascade

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study employed Chinese pediatric atlases (CHN-PD) for registration and segmentation, which is appropriate for the Chinese Asian population studied. Sex-stratified analyses were performed (Supplementary Figs. S4 and S5) showing different patterns between males and females in patient groups. The study noted that most children were scanned under sedation (chloral hydrate), with only a small minority scanned during natural sleep or awake (2/563 ASD with DD/ID, 1/212 ASD without DD/ID, 1/36 DD/ID, 21/219 TD). Functional network-level analyses were performed by mapping deviations to Yeo-7 networks, showing common abnormalities in default mode, ventral attention, somatomotor, and visual networks, with high heterogeneity in limbic and visual networks. Gene enrichment analysis was performed using multiple databases (GO, KEGG) via Metascape.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a large pediatric neuroimaging study (N=1030, age 1-7 years) from China focusing on very young children with ASD and DD/ID. The study is notable for: (1) Using normative modeling to quantify individual deviations rather than group-level comparisons; (2) Distinguishing three patient subgroups (ASD with DD/ID, ASD without DD/ID, DD/ID only); (3) Multi-scale analysis linking brain asymmetry to both clinical phenotypes and gene expression; (4) Use of population-specific (Chinese) pediatric brain atlases; (5) Two-site data collection with harmonization; (6) Extensive clinical characterization with multiple instruments (ADOS, CARS, ABC, SRS, SM, GDS/IQ). The discrepancy between 219 TD children mentioned in Methods/Participants and 247 TDs used for normative model training is not clearly explained. Data from two sites: Site 1 (Philips Ingenia, n=283: 164 ASD+DD/ID, 74 ASD, 0 DD/ID, 45 TD) and Site 2 (Siemens Verio, n=747: 399 ASD+DD/ID, 138 ASD, 36 DD/ID, 174 TD). The study emphasizes heterogeneity in ASD, with kurtosis analysis revealing extreme individual variability in specific regions. Cross-validation results showed high correlations (>0.948) between original and validation fold deviations. The study was approved by Xinhua Hospital Ethics Committee (XHEC-C-2019-076) and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04358744).
